cards.statement: A normal declaration in a user style sheet overrides a normal author declaration on the same element.
cards.explanation: Normal author declarations outrank normal user declarations. The browser resolves origin precedence before it compares selectors.
cards.misconception: Normal user styles outrank normal author styles.

cards.statement: An important user-agent declaration outranks an important declaration in a user style sheet.
cards.explanation: Important declarations reverse the ordinary origin order, giving user-agent important declarations precedence over user important declarations.

cards.statement: A running CSS animation's value outranks a normal declaration in the element's style attribute.
cards.explanation: Animation values sit above normal author declarations in the cascade, including normal declarations attached through a style attribute.

cards.statement: An author declaration marked `!important` outranks the value supplied by an active CSS transition.
cards.explanation: During an active CSS transition, its generated value has higher cascade precedence than important declarations.
cards.misconception: Important declarations outrank active transition values.

cards.statement: A style attribute declaration outranks an author style rule when both have the same importance.
cards.explanation: The cascade gives element-attached declarations priority over author style rules of the same importance.

cards.statement: CSS inheritance passes the parent's used property value to its child.
cards.explanation: Inheritance transfers the parent's computed value. A used value includes later layout calculations.
cards.misconception: Inheritance transfers layout-resolved used values.

cards.statement: On the root element, `color: inherit` resolves to the property's initial value.
cards.explanation: The root has no parent from which to inherit. Explicit inheritance on the root therefore supplies the property's initial value.

cards.statement: `display: initial` on a `div` gives it the browser's default `block` display.
cards.explanation: The initial display value is inline. In ordinary flow, display: revert instead rolls back author styling and recovers the browser's block value for a div.
cards.misconception: initial restores element-specific browser stylesheet values.

cards.statement: With `margin: inherit`, a child takes its parent's computed margin values.
cards.explanation: The inherit keyword makes an element take the computed value of a property from its parent. Margin is a non-inherited property, so this keyword is how a child copies it.

cards.statement: `color: unset` selects the inherited color value for an element with a parent.
cards.explanation: The unset keyword follows the property's normal inheritance behavior. Color is an inherited property.

cards.statement: `all: initial` resets an element's unregistered custom properties to their initial values.
cards.explanation: The all shorthand leaves custom properties unchanged. It also excludes direction and unicode-bidi.
cards.misconception: The all shorthand includes custom properties.

cards.statement: Reopening a named `@layer` keeps the layer in the position established by its first appearance.
cards.explanation: A later block for an existing layer appends rules to that layer. Its position in the layer order stays fixed.

cards.statement: A normal ID rule in an earlier layer outranks a normal type rule in a later layer.
cards.explanation: For competing normal author declarations, the later layer wins before the browser considers selector specificity.
cards.misconception: An ID selector overcomes a lower-priority cascade layer.

cards.statement: An unlayered important author declaration outranks a layered important author declaration.
cards.explanation: Within the author origin, important declarations in layers have precedence over important declarations outside layers.
cards.misconception: Unlayered declarations have highest priority even when important.

cards.statement: `revert-layer` restores an earlier declaration for the property in its current cascade layer.
cards.explanation: The revert-layer keyword removes its layer's contribution for the property and exposes lower-priority layers or the previous origin.
cards.misconception: revert-layer retries earlier declarations in the same layer.

source.title: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 5: revert-layer

cards.statement: A top-level `@import` after an `@layer` block remains a valid stylesheet import.
cards.explanation: An @import after an @layer block is ignored. Layer statements, such as @layer theme;, are allowed before imports.
cards.misconception: The placement exception for layer statements also covers layer blocks.

cards.statement: `@scope (.card) to (.footer)` includes the matching scope-limit elements in its scope.
cards.explanation: An @scope lower boundary excludes the matched scope-limit elements and their descendants from the scope.
cards.misconception: The lower scope boundary includes its matched elements.

cards.statement: The bare `p` selector inside `@scope (#card)` keeps specificity 0-0-1.
cards.explanation: The scope-root selector sets the scope boundary rather than contributing to the specificity of a bare scoped selector.

cards.statement: An explicit `:scope` in a scoped selector adds 0-1-0 to selector specificity.
cards.explanation: The :scope pseudo-class contributes class-level weight when an author writes it explicitly in the selector.

cards.statement: Within one author layer, scope proximity takes precedence over selector specificity.
cards.explanation: The browser compares specificity before scope proximity. Proximity resolves competing declarations with equal specificity.
cards.misconception: A nearer scope root overcomes a more specific competing selector.

cards.statement: Inherited values from a scoped rule continue to descendants beyond its scope limit.
cards.explanation: Scope boundaries constrain selector matching. Inherited properties still pass values down the element tree beyond those boundaries.

cards.statement: The selector `[id="panel"]` contributes 0-1-0 to specificity.
cards.explanation: An attribute selector adds class-column weight even when the attribute being tested is id.

cards.statement: The `::before` pseudo-element adds weight to the CLASS column of specificity.
cards.explanation: A pseudo-element contributes to the TYPE column, with weight 0-0-1.
cards.misconception: Pseudo-elements carry the same specificity weight as ordinary pseudo-classes.

cards.statement: The universal selector `*` adds 0-0-1 to a selector's specificity.
cards.explanation: The universal selector contributes zero specificity, regardless of the elements it matches.
cards.misconception: Matching any element gives the universal selector type-column weight.

cards.statement: A child combinator `>` contributes zero weight to a selector's specificity.
cards.explanation: Combinators restrict relationships between matched elements, but add no weight to the specificity calculation.

cards.statement: One ID selector has greater specificity than a selector containing eleven classes.
cards.explanation: Specificity compares the ID column before the CLASS column. Counts in a later column do not carry into an earlier one.

cards.statement: `:is(.item, #panel)` has specificity 0-1-0 when the `.item` branch matches.
cards.explanation: The selector :is(.item, #panel) has specificity 1-0-0. The ID's weight applies even when .item is the matching branch.
cards.misconception: These selector functions use matching-branch specificity.

cards.statement: `:where(#panel .item)` contributes zero specificity despite the ID in its argument.
cards.explanation: The :where() function gives itself and its arguments zero specificity.

cards.statement: `:nth-child(2 of .item)` has the same specificity as `.item`.
cards.explanation: The selector :nth-child(2 of .item) has specificity 0-2-0: one pseudo-class weight plus the class weight from its of argument.
cards.misconception: The of selector replaces rather than adds to nth-child's own weight.

cards.statement: In `.card, #panel { & .title {} }`, `&` uses class-level weight when the parent matches `.card`.
cards.explanation: The nesting selector takes the greatest specificity in the parent selector list. Here the ID sets the weight of & to 1-0-0.
cards.misconception: The nesting selector uses the weight of the matching parent-list branch.

cards.statement: For normal unlayered author rules, a more specific selector wins over a later less specific selector.
cards.explanation: For competing declarations in that cascade group, the browser compares specificity before order of appearance.

cards.statement: A `p` color declaration beats a color inherited from a parent's ID rule.
cards.explanation: A declaration targeting the paragraph supplies its own color value. The parent's selector weight does not accompany an inherited value.

cards.statement: A `div`'s background color fills the margin area surrounding its border box.
cards.explanation: A box's background painting area stops at the outer border edge by default. Its margin lies outside that area.
cards.misconception: The margin area belongs to the element's background painting area.

source.title: Introduction to the CSS box model

cards.statement: `box-sizing: initial` makes `width` size the content box.
cards.explanation: The initial value of box-sizing is content-box, so the width applies to the content area.

cards.statement: With `box-sizing: border-box`, `width` includes the element's margins.
cards.explanation: Border-box sizing includes content, padding and borders in the specified width. Margins remain outside that width.
cards.misconception: Border-box sizing includes margins in width.

cards.statement: A child's `box-sizing` follows its parent's computed value through CSS inheritance.
cards.explanation: Box-sizing is a non-inherited property. A child's value comes from its own declarations or defaulting.
cards.misconception: Setting box-sizing on a parent propagates it to children.

cards.statement: A border-box content width stays at zero when padding and borders exceed the specified width.
cards.explanation: The browser floors the content width at zero. Padding and borders can make the resulting border box exceed the requested width.

cards.statement: Percentage `padding-top` uses the containing block's height as its reference.
cards.explanation: Percentage padding uses the containing block's inline size, which is its width in the assumed horizontal writing mode.
cards.misconception: Percentage top padding is relative to containing-block height.

cards.statement: Auto left and right margins center a fixed-width block in ordinary flow when horizontal space remains.
cards.explanation: The block layout algorithm distributes the remaining horizontal space equally between its two auto margins.

cards.statement: When `min-width` exceeds `max-width`, the minimum width wins.
cards.explanation: A conflicting maximum width does not force the used width below the specified minimum width.

cards.statement: `aspect-ratio: 2 / 1` on an empty block `div` with `width: 300px` and `height: auto` gives it a 150px height.
cards.explanation: With one automatic dimension, the browser derives it from the other through the ratio: 300px / 2 = 150px. When width and height are both set to lengths, aspect-ratio has no effect on the box.

cards.statement: `inline-size` controls a box's physical width in a vertical writing mode.
cards.explanation: In a vertical writing mode, inline-size maps to physical height because the inline axis runs vertically.
cards.misconception: inline-size maps to physical width regardless of writing mode.

cards.statement: With horizontal writing and RTL direction, `margin-inline-start` sets the right margin.
cards.explanation: The inline-start edge follows text direction. With right-to-left horizontal text, that edge is on the right.

source.title: Logical properties for margins, borders, and padding

cards.statement: With spare main-axis space, `justify-content: flex-start` aligns a `row-reverse` flex line at the left edge.
cards.explanation: In the assumed left-to-right writing direction, row-reverse puts main-start on the right. Flex-start aligns the items at that main-start edge.
cards.misconception: flex-start names a fixed physical left edge.

source.title: Aligning items in a flex container

cards.statement: `display: flex` gives an element a block-level outer display type in ordinary flow.
cards.explanation: The flex keyword equals the multi-keyword value block flex: the outer type block makes the container block-level in its parent's flow, while the inner type flex lays out its children.

source.title: Using the multi-keyword syntax with CSS display

cards.statement: `display: inline-block` and `display: inline flow-root` give a box the same display types.
cards.explanation: Both forms give the box an inline outer display type and a flow-root inner display type.

source.title: Using the multi-keyword syntax with CSS display

cards.statement: `width: 200px` gives a non-replaced inline box a 200px content width.
cards.explanation: The width property does not apply to non-replaced inline boxes. Their inline contents determine their width.
cards.misconception: The width property fixes the width of an ordinary inline box.

cards.statement: `visibility: hidden` preserves an in-flow box's place in the surrounding layout.
cards.explanation: The hidden value hides the box while retaining its normal contribution to layout.

cards.statement: `overflow: clip` establishes a new block formatting context for a normal-flow block.
cards.explanation: The clip overflow value does not establish a block formatting context by itself.
cards.misconception: Clipping overflow establishes a block formatting context.

cards.statement: An auto-height `display: flow-root` block accounts for its floating children's height.
cards.explanation: A flow-root box establishes a block formatting context, so its auto height accounts for its internal floats.

cards.statement: Text inside a new block formatting context wraps its line boxes around a float outside that context.
cards.explanation: An external float stays outside a new block formatting context. Its box may move or narrow, but its internal line boxes do not wrap around that float.
cards.misconception: An external float intrudes into a separate block formatting context's line layout.

cards.statement: When adjoining positive margins of normal-flow block siblings collapse, the larger margin sets their separation.
cards.explanation: The collapsed margin between adjoining block siblings equals the larger of their two positive margins.

cards.statement: A parent's positive top padding separates its top margin from its first in-flow block child's top margin.
cards.explanation: Positive top padding lies between those parent and child margins, preventing that pair from collapsing.

cards.statement: When one positive and one negative margin collapse, the browser keeps the one with the larger absolute value.
cards.explanation: For a collapsing pair with one positive and one negative margin, the browser adds the two signed values.
cards.misconception: Mixed-sign margin collapse chooses the margin with the larger magnitude.

cards.statement: Sibling flex items collapse their adjoining vertical margins in a container with `flex-direction: column`.
cards.explanation: Margins between flex items stay separate, including in a column flex container. Flex layout suppresses margin collapsing between its items.
cards.misconception: Vertically stacked flex items use ordinary block margin collapsing.

source.title: CSS Flexible Box Layout Module Level 1

cards.statement: A relatively positioned block keeps its original layout space when an inset shifts its visible position.
cards.explanation: Relative positioning offsets a box after normal layout. Surrounding boxes keep the space allocated for its original position.

cards.statement: An absolute child of a `position: relative` block is positioned against that parent's content box.
cards.explanation: An absolutely positioned box's containing block is the padding box of its nearest positioned ancestor, so its offsets are measured from inside the border, padding included.
cards.misconception: An absolute child's containing block excludes its positioned parent's padding.

cards.statement: A fixed child of a block with `transform: translateX(10px)` is positioned relative to the viewport.
cards.explanation: The transformed block establishes the containing block for its fixed child, so the child is positioned relative to that block.
cards.misconception: Fixed positioning retains a viewport containing block inside a transformed ancestor.

cards.statement: A static block uses its ordinary `display: inline` parent's content box as its containing block.
cards.explanation: The browser uses the content box of the nearest block-container ancestor or formatting-context root, skipping an ordinary inline parent.
cards.misconception: A static block uses its direct parent as its containing block regardless of that parent's display type.

cards.statement: `top: 10%` on an absolutely positioned box uses its containing block's height as the percentage reference.
cards.explanation: A percentage top inset is relative to the containing block's height.

cards.statement: A sticky box with `top: auto` and `bottom: auto` sticks vertically when its scrolling ancestor scrolls.
cards.explanation: With both vertical inset values set to auto, sticky behaves as relative positioning on that axis. A non-auto top or bottom supplies a vertical threshold.
cards.misconception: Sticky positioning supplies a vertical threshold when both vertical insets are auto.

cards.statement: A sticky box in an `overflow: hidden` ancestor with nothing to scroll sticks to that ancestor instead of the viewport.
cards.explanation: Sticky positioning attaches to the nearest ancestor with a scrolling mechanism (overflow hidden, scroll, auto or overlay), even if that ancestor never actually scrolls.

cards.statement: A sticky box's containing block limits its movement as its scrolling ancestor continues to scroll.
cards.explanation: Sticky positioning keeps the box constrained by its containing block. Further scrolling cannot keep it pinned beyond that block's boundary.

cards.statement: An ordinary block with `position: relative; z-index: auto` creates a stacking context through positioning.
cards.explanation: Relative positioning alone does not create a stacking context. Its z-index needs a value other than auto for positioning to create one.
cards.misconception: Relative positioning creates a stacking context even with an auto z-index.

cards.statement: `z-index` controls the stacking of flex and grid items whose `position` is `static`.
cards.explanation: Flex and grid items use z-index for their stack level even while statically positioned. Their item status makes z-index applicable.

cards.statement: A descendant's high `z-index` outranks a sibling context stacked above its parent's stacking context.
cards.explanation: The browser stacks each context as one unit in its parent context. A child's z-index changes its place inside that unit rather than raising the unit among siblings.
cards.misconception: A descendant's z-index escapes the stacking order of its ancestor's context.

cards.statement: `isolation: isolate` creates a stacking context for a block whose `z-index` is `auto`.
cards.explanation: The isolate value explicitly establishes a stacking context, independently of the block's z-index.

cards.statement: A flex container's initial `flex-wrap` value moves excess items onto additional flex lines.
cards.explanation: The initial flex-wrap value is nowrap. Items remain on one flex line even when that line overflows.
cards.misconception: Flex containers wrap overflowing items by default.

cards.statement: By default, a row flex item with `height: auto` and zero margins stretches to its flex line's height.
cards.explanation: The initial align-items value is stretch: an item whose cross size computes to auto and whose cross-axis margins are not auto fills the line, within its min and max sizes.

source.title: CSS Flexible Box Layout Module Level 1

cards.statement: By default, a flex item's `flex-grow` value lets it expand into positive free space.
cards.explanation: The initial flex-grow value is 0. A flex item starts with zero participation in the distribution of positive free space.
cards.misconception: Flex items grow into free space by default.

cards.statement: `flex: 1` sets a flex item's flex-basis to zero instead of auto.
cards.explanation: A single unitless number sets flex-grow to that number, flex-shrink to 1 and flex-basis to zero (MDN writes 0%). The keyword flex: auto keeps the auto basis instead.

cards.statement: Equal `flex-shrink` values produce equal pixel reductions for items with different flex base sizes.
cards.explanation: Flexbox weights negative-space sharing by each item's flex-shrink multiplied by its flex base size, subject to sizing limits.
cards.misconception: Equal shrink factors produce equal pixel reductions despite different base sizes.

source.title: Controlling ratios of flex items along the main axis

cards.statement: `min-width: 0` lets a row flex item with `overflow: visible` shrink below its contents' min-content width.
cards.explanation: For a row flex item with visible overflow, min-width: 0 removes the automatic content minimum that would otherwise limit shrinking.

cards.statement: `align-content: center` packs the line at cross-axis center in a `flex-wrap: nowrap` container.
cards.explanation: align-content has no effect in a flex-wrap: nowrap container. Its line distribution applies to wrapping flex containers.
cards.misconception: align-content aligns the line in a nowrap flex container.

cards.statement: A flex item's auto margins absorb positive free space before Flexbox applies alignment.
cards.explanation: Flexbox gives positive free space to auto margins before alignment. Those margins consume the space that alignment would otherwise distribute.

source.title: CSS Flexible Box Layout Module Level 1

cards.statement: `float: left` takes a flex item out of the layout its flex container uses for other items.
cards.explanation: A flex item stays in the flex layout when float: left is set. The float declaration does not make that item float or remove it from flow.
cards.misconception: A float declaration removes a flex item from flex layout.

source.title: CSS Flexible Box Layout Module Level 1

cards.statement: `gap: 12px` adds spacing between a flex container's border and its outermost items.
cards.explanation: Flex gap creates gutters between items and between flex lines. It does not add a gutter at the container's outer edges.
cards.misconception: Flex gap adds padding-like space at the container's edges.

cards.statement: Grid's `fr` tracks divide the full container width, including space reserved for fixed tracks.
cards.explanation: Fractional tracks share leftover space after fixed track sizes and gutters are accounted for. They do not divide the container's entire width.
cards.misconception: Fractional tracks divide total container space before fixed sizes are deducted.

cards.statement: `repeat(auto-fill, 1fr)` creates as many equal fractional columns as fit in a grid container.
cards.explanation: auto-fill requires a fixed-size track definition; bare 1fr does not qualify. A bounded form such as minmax(100px, 1fr) qualifies.
cards.misconception: Bare fractional tracks are valid inside an auto-fill repetition.

cards.statement: With `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(100px, 1fr))`, two items in a wide container stretch across the full row.
cards.explanation: auto-fit collapses repeated tracks still empty after placement to 0px, along with their gutters, so the two filled 1fr tracks share the freed space.

cards.statement: Grid line -1 marks the final line of implicit tracks added after the explicit grid.
cards.explanation: Negative grid line numbers count from the end of the explicit grid. Added implicit tracks do not move the line identified by -1.
cards.misconception: Negative grid lines are counted from the end of the implicit grid.

cards.statement: A name in `grid-template-areas` can form an L-shaped area across adjoining grid cells.
cards.explanation: Repeated names in grid-template-areas have to form rectangles. An L-shaped named area makes that declaration invalid.
cards.misconception: A named grid area accepts a non-rectangular shape.

cards.statement: `justify-items: center` aligns grid items along the inline axis within their grid areas.
cards.explanation: The property aligns each item within its own grid area on the inline axis, which is horizontal in the assumed writing mode.

cards.statement: `grid-template-columns: subgrid` uses the parent grid's column tracks across the item's span.
cards.explanation: A subgrid's column dimension uses the parent tracks covered by the grid item's span. It shares their sizing instead of defining an independent column list.

cards.statement: In a subgridded dimension, `gap: normal` gives the subgrid zero spacing between its tracks.
cards.explanation: In a subgridded dimension, normal gap uses the parent's gutter size.
cards.misconception: normal gap resolves to zero in a subgridded dimension.

cards.statement: Children of a subgrid can use the parent's line names within the subgridded span.
cards.explanation: Parent line names are available on corresponding subgrid lines. Placement rules inside the subgrid can reference those names.

cards.statement: A subgrid adds implicit tracks along a subgridded axis when its children exceed its span.
cards.explanation: A subgridded dimension has no implicit tracks. Extra children use the existing tracks rather than extending that subgridded axis.
cards.misconception: Subgrid creates implicit tracks along an axis inherited from its parent.

cards.statement: `width: 1in` and `width: 96px` specify the same CSS length.
cards.explanation: CSS fixes the ratio between its absolute length units: one inch equals 96 CSS pixels.

cards.statement: An element's `font-size: 2em` bases its length on that element's computed font size.
cards.explanation: Inside font-size, the em unit uses the element's inherited font size. A 2em font size doubles that inherited size.
cards.misconception: The em unit uses the element's own computed font size even inside font-size.

cards.statement: A nested element's `padding: 1rem` uses the root element's font size as its length reference.
cards.explanation: The rem unit refers to the root element's font size, so deeper nesting leaves this padding's font-size reference unchanged.

cards.statement: `width: 20ch` sizes an element using its font's average character width.
cards.explanation: The ch unit uses the advance width of the font's zero glyph, rather than an average across its characters.
cards.misconception: The ch unit measures an average character width.

cards.statement: `height: 1lh` follows the height of the element's actual line box when its content changes.
cards.explanation: The lh unit uses the element's computed line-height converted to a length. Content may enlarge an actual line box beyond that reference.
cards.misconception: The lh unit measures actual line boxes after their contents affect layout.

source.title: CSS Values and Units Module Level 4

cards.statement: A child inherits a unitless `line-height` as a factor applied to its own font size.
cards.explanation: A unitless line-height keeps the number as its computed value. The child multiplies that inherited number by its own font size.

cards.statement: `height: 100svh` uses the viewport height with the browser's retractable interface expanded.
cards.explanation: The small viewport height assumes the browser's retractable interface is expanded, reserving the space occupied by that interface.

source.title: CSS Values and Units Module Level 4

cards.statement: `height: 100dvh` retains its original length after retracting browser chrome enlarges the available viewport.
cards.explanation: The dvh unit follows the dynamic viewport height. Its reference updates when retracting browser chrome changes the available viewport height.
cards.misconception: Dynamic viewport units retain their initial length after retractable browser interface changes the available viewport.

source.title: CSS Values and Units Module Level 4

cards.statement: The browser's fallback reference for an element's `cqw` length is the small viewport's width.
cards.explanation: If the browser finds no eligible query container for cqw, it uses the small viewport width as the reference instead.

cards.statement: `calc(100% -20px)` subtracts 20px from a percentage when the browser parses the expression.
cards.explanation: The subtraction operator in calc() needs whitespace on both sides. In calc(100% -20px), the browser reads a negative length rather than a subtraction operator.
cards.misconception: An adjacent minus sign acts as calc() subtraction with whitespace on just one side.

cards.statement: `width: calc(0 + 20px)` computes to a length of 20px.
cards.explanation: A bare 0 inside calc() is a number, so adding it to 20px mixes incompatible types. Writing 0px supplies the length type needed for this addition.
cards.misconception: Unitless zero acts as a length inside calc() addition.

cards.statement: The browser treats `--accent` and `--Accent` as names for the same custom property.
cards.explanation: Custom property names are case-sensitive. The browser keeps --accent and --Accent as two separate properties.
cards.misconception: Custom property names follow the case-insensitive matching of ordinary CSS property names.

cards.statement: An unspecified, unregistered custom property on a child inherits the parent's value.
cards.explanation: Unregistered custom properties inherit, so a parent's value reaches a child whose own cascade supplies no value.

cards.statement: In `var(--fonts, Arial, sans-serif)`, `Arial, sans-serif` is one fallback value.
cards.explanation: The first comma separates the custom property name from its fallback. The remaining tokens, including further commas, belong to that fallback.

cards.statement: With `--n: 8`, `width: var(--n)px` substitutes a valid length into the width declaration.
cards.explanation: var() substitutes tokens rather than joining their text. The number token and px identifier stay separate; calc(var(--n) * 1px) produces a length.
cards.misconception: A number supplied by var() joins a following unit into a length token.

source.title: CSS Custom Properties for Cascading Variables Module Level 1

cards.statement: On a child, a `color` declaration made invalid by `var()` substitution restores an earlier valid declaration.
cards.explanation: Invalid var() substitution is discovered after the cascade chooses a declaration. For color on a child, the browser inherits its parent's value instead of retrying an earlier declaration.
cards.misconception: Computed-value invalidity makes the cascade retry an earlier declaration.

cards.statement: `@media (min-width: var(--breakpoint))` uses the custom property's value as its breakpoint.
cards.explanation: var() substitutes values in declarations on elements. It does not substitute a custom property's value into a media query condition.
cards.misconception: Custom property substitution works inside media query conditions.

cards.statement: A dependency cycle between unregistered custom properties makes their values invalid at computed-value time.
cards.explanation: The browser detects cycles in custom property references on an element. Properties participating in a cycle compute to the guaranteed-invalid value.

source.title: CSS Custom Properties for Cascading Variables Module Level 1

cards.statement: For an undeclared `--gap` registered as `<length>` with an initial-value, `var(--gap, 1rem)` returns that initial-value.
cards.explanation: A registered property with a non-universal syntax and an initial-value substitutes that initial value when no other declaration applies, so var() leaves the 1rem fallback unused.

cards.statement: An `@property` rule with `syntax: "*"` needs an `initial-value` descriptor for a valid registration.
cards.explanation: The initial-value descriptor is optional when @property uses the universal syntax "*".
cards.misconception: The initial-value descriptor is mandatory even with universal syntax.

cards.statement: For `@property` with `syntax: "<length>"`, `initial-value: 2em` is a valid registration value.
cards.explanation: A non-universal registration's initial value has to be computationally independent. An em length depends on font sizing, so this initial value invalidates the rule.
cards.misconception: A type-matching initial value is sufficient even when its computation depends on font sizing.

cards.statement: A valid `CSS.registerProperty()` registration takes precedence over `@property` for the same name.
cards.explanation: When JavaScript and CSS register the same custom property name, the browser uses the JavaScript registration.

cards.statement: A custom property registered with `syntax: "<length>"` interpolates as a length during a transition.
cards.explanation: The registered syntax gives the custom property's computed values a type. A transition interpolates those values using that type's rules.

source.title: CSS Properties and Values API Level 1

cards.statement: `article > p` matches a paragraph whose immediate parent is an article.
cards.explanation: The > relationship connects a paragraph to its immediate article parent. An intervening ancestor places the paragraph outside this selector's match.

cards.statement: `h2 + p` skips intervening div siblings while selecting the next paragraph.
cards.explanation: h2 + p matches a paragraph immediately following an h2 in the element-sibling sequence. An intervening div breaks that adjacency.
cards.misconception: The next-sibling combinator skips non-matching element siblings.

cards.statement: `h2 ~ p` matches a paragraph later in the h2's parent's child list.
cards.explanation: The h2 and p have to share a parent, with the paragraph later in that parent's child list.

cards.statement: `:is()` and `:where()` keep valid selectors usable when another argument selector is invalid.
cards.explanation: Both pseudo-classes use forgiving selector lists. The browser discards invalid entries while using the valid entries that remain.

cards.statement: `h2:has(+ p)` selects the paragraph that immediately follows a sibling h2.
cards.explanation: h2:has(+ p) selects the heading, using the following paragraph as a condition. The element before :has() remains the styling target.
cards.misconception: A relational pseudo-class selects the element mentioned in its argument.

cards.statement: `:nth-child(2 of .selected)` counts siblings of any class when finding the second position.
cards.explanation: The of .selected filter limits counting to matching siblings. :nth-child(2 of .selected) selects the second matching sibling even when its overall child index differs.
cards.misconception: The of selector filters the final match after counting the whole element-sibling list.

cards.statement: A nested `p { ... }` rule inside `.card { ... }` targets paragraphs descended from a card.
cards.explanation: The browser accepts the nested type selector p and supplies the parent context, giving it the matching behavior of .card p.

cards.statement: The nested selector `&:hover` inside `.card` targets a hovered descendant of the card.
cards.explanation: In a .card rule, &:hover matches the card itself while it is hovered. The ampersand attaches the pseudo-class to the parent selector.
cards.misconception: An attached nesting selector applies a pseudo-class to descendants.

cards.statement: The nested selector `.theme &` inside `.card` matches cards descended from a .theme element.
cards.explanation: Appending & after .theme puts the parent selector after that ancestor context, so the nested selector matches like .theme .card.

cards.statement: In native CSS nesting, `&__title` inside `.card` creates the selector `.card__title`.
cards.explanation: The nesting selector represents an element selector, not a text prefix. Native CSS treats &__title as invalid instead of joining it to .card.
cards.misconception: The nesting selector concatenates text onto the parent's class name.

cards.statement: CSS hoists declarations written after a nested rule ahead of that rule when resolving source order.
cards.explanation: Declarations after a nested rule retain their written position. The nested declarations rule preserves their place in the cascade's order of appearance.
cards.misconception: The browser hoists declarations that follow nested rules ahead of those rules.

cards.statement: `@media (hover: hover), (pointer: fine)` combines its conditions with logical AND.
cards.explanation: A comma separates alternatives in a media query list. This query matches when either condition matches.
cards.misconception: Comma-separated media queries require both conditions to match.

cards.statement: A media query with an unknown media type treats that type as `all`.
cards.explanation: An unknown media type evaluates to false. The browser does not substitute the all media type for it.
cards.misconception: An unknown media type falls back to matching any medium.

cards.statement: An `em` value in a media query uses the computed `font-size` of the document's root element.
cards.explanation: In a media query, em uses the initial font-size defined by the browser or user preferences. Page font-size declarations do not change this reference.
cards.misconception: Media query font-relative units follow the page's root font size.

cards.statement: Setting `color-scheme: dark` on a top-level page's root makes `(prefers-color-scheme: dark)` match.
cards.explanation: On a top-level page, prefers-color-scheme reflects the user's preference from operating-system or browser settings. A CSS declaration does not set that preference.
cards.misconception: The page's color-scheme declaration sets the preference queried by prefers-color-scheme.

cards.statement: The `pointer` media feature bases its result on the browser's selected primary pointing device.
cards.explanation: When several pointing devices are available, pointer targets the primary device selected by the browser.

cards.statement: An `inline-size` query container ignores its contents when calculating its intrinsic inline size.
cards.explanation: Inline-size containment removes the contents' contribution to the container's intrinsic inline size, breaking a size dependency on its children.

cards.statement: A size query on an element measures that element when it has `container-type: size`.
cards.explanation: A size query selects an eligible ancestor container of the element being styled. Giving the styled element container-type: size does not make it query itself.
cards.misconception: An element becomes the subject of its own size query when marked as a size container.

cards.statement: `@container sidebar (width > 20em)` skips nearer size containers with `container-name: main`.
cards.explanation: The name filters eligible ancestor containers. This query selects the nearest eligible one that includes sidebar among its container names.

source.title: Using container size and style queries

cards.statement: `container: sidebar` preserves an element's existing `container-type: inline-size` setting.
cards.explanation: The container shorthand resets an omitted container-type to normal. Setting the name alone replaces an earlier inline-size setting.
cards.misconception: Omitting the type from the container shorthand preserves its earlier longhand value.

cards.statement: A `div` with `container-type: normal` is eligible for `style(--theme: dark)` queries.
cards.explanation: A div with normal container-type remains a style query container. Descendants can query its custom property values with style().

source.title: Using container size and style queries

cards.statement: A `<color>`-registered `--c` set to `#0000ff` matches `style(--c: blue)`.
cards.explanation: Registering the property with <color> syntax lets style() treat equivalent values as a match, so blue, #00f and rgb(0 0 255) all match. Unregistered, the tokens are compared as written.

source.title: Using container size and style queries

cards.statement: In eight-digit CSS hex notation, the first pair of digits sets the color's alpha.
cards.explanation: Eight-digit CSS hex colors put alpha in the last pair: #RRGGBBAA. The first pair specifies the red channel.
cards.misconception: CSS hex colors place alpha before the red, green and blue channels.

cards.statement: Modern space-separated `rgb()` separates alpha from the color channels with a comma.
cards.explanation: Modern rgb() puts a slash before alpha, as in rgb(20 40 60 / 0.5). A comma before alpha belongs to the legacy comma-separated syntax.
cards.misconception: Modern rgb() uses a comma before alpha while separating its color channels with spaces.

cards.statement: The first channel of `oklch()` uses a scale designed to follow perceived lightness.
cards.explanation: Oklch takes its L coordinate from Oklab's perceptual lightness model. It describes perceived lightness rather than the HSL lightness parameter.

cards.statement: `oklch()` and `hsl()` share one hue wheel for their hue angles.
cards.explanation: Hue angles differ between color spaces: hsl() works in sRGB while oklch() works in Oklab, so the same angle can name a different hue in each function.
cards.misconception: oklch() hue angles map to the same hues as hsl() hue angles.

cards.statement: In `oklch()`, a chroma of 100% represents the numeric chroma value 0.4.
cards.explanation: Oklch uses 0.4 as the reference for chroma percentages, so number and percentage forms use different scales.

cards.statement: Changing `color(srgb 1 0 0)` to `color(display-p3 1 0 0)` preserves the specified color.
cards.explanation: The red primaries of sRGB and Display P3 differ. Changing the space name reinterprets the channel coordinates instead of converting the existing color.
cards.misconception: Changing color()'s color-space name converts unchanged channel numbers to preserve the original color.

source.title: CSS Color Module Level 4: Predefined color spaces

cards.statement: `color-mix(in oklab, red, blue)` gives the two input colors equal shares of the mix.
cards.explanation: With both color percentages omitted, this two-color Oklab mix assigns 50% to red and 50% to blue.

cards.statement: With opaque inputs, `color-mix(in srgb, red 20%, blue 20%)` produces an opaque result.
cards.explanation: This sRGB mix normalizes the color shares, then multiplies the result's alpha by their original total of 40%. The resulting alpha is 0.4.
cards.misconception: Normalizing color-mix() percentages to equal shares preserves full opacity despite a total below 100%.

cards.statement: In `oklch(from red l c h)`, the `l` channel keyword resolves to a percentage for calculations.
cards.explanation: Relative color channel keywords resolve to numbers. The l keyword stays a number even when the origin color specifies lightness as a percentage.
cards.misconception: Relative color channel keywords keep the unit types accepted by their color function's normal syntax.

cards.statement: `rgb(from var(--base) r g b)` keeps the alpha of the color stored in `--base`.
cards.explanation: Relative rgb() uses its origin color's alpha when the output alpha is omitted. Reusing the three color channels leaves that alpha intact.

cards.statement: In `animation: fade 2s 1s`, the browser assigns the first time value to the delay.
cards.explanation: In animation: fade 2s 1s, the first time value sets animation-duration to 2s. The second sets animation-delay to 1s.
cards.misconception: The first time value in the animation shorthand specifies its delay.

cards.statement: When a discrete property changes, `transition-behavior: normal` starts a transition for its set duration.
cards.explanation: The normal value skips transitions for discrete properties. The allow-discrete value makes those properties eligible for timed transitions.
cards.misconception: The normal transition behavior starts transitions for discrete properties.

cards.statement: During an entry transition, `display` flips from `none` to `block` at the midpoint like other discrete values.
cards.explanation: For an entry transition from display: none to block, display switches at the start. The box remains displayed throughout the transition.
cards.misconception: Display entry transitions switch values at the ordinary discrete midpoint.

cards.statement: `@starting-style { .box { opacity: 0 } }` outranks a later `.box { opacity: 1 }` for starting values.
cards.explanation: The .box selectors inside and outside @starting-style have equal specificity. A later .box rule overrides the starting values, so place the standalone @starting-style rule after it.
cards.misconception: A starting-style rule has special priority over later regular rules with the same selector.

cards.statement: An animation's omitted 0% keyframe takes its values from the element's existing styles.
cards.explanation: The browser supplies an omitted starting keyframe from the element's existing property values, rather than substituting those properties' initial values.

cards.statement: A declaration marked `!important` inside a keyframe drops out of that animation's keyframe values.
cards.explanation: Keyframe rules discard important declarations, leaving the remaining declarations to supply that animation's values.

cards.statement: Within one `@keyframes` rule, repeated 50% blocks contribute their declarations to the same keyframe.
cards.explanation: The browser combines declarations from blocks at the same offset within one @keyframes rule. If declarations conflict, the later one wins.

cards.statement: `animation-fill-mode: forwards` keeps the ending computed values of a completed finite animation.
cards.explanation: With animation-fill-mode: forwards, the animation's ending values stay in effect after its active time ends, while the animation remains applied.

cards.statement: With `animation-direction: alternate`, the browser plays the first iteration in reverse.
cards.explanation: animation-direction: alternate begins with a forward iteration. It reverses direction on the following iteration.
cards.misconception: The alternate direction begins with a reverse iteration.

cards.statement: `translate: 50px` with `transform: rotate(45deg)` renders like `transform: translate(50px) rotate(45deg)`.
cards.explanation: The browser composes translate, rotate and scale first, then multiplies in the transform list, so the individual properties act as if written to the left of the transform functions.
